title: The Practitioner paper: scenario, additional information, classic and matching
blurb: Know exactly how the 70-mark paper is built, so every minute goes on judgement, not on working out the format.
question: You open the paper and see a scenario booklet, a page of named people and 70 numbered questions, some sharing one list of headings. How is it marked, and how should you use each part?

teach.body: The PRINCE2 7 Practitioner exam gives you a scenario booklet describing one project, plus a section of additional information about the people who might work on it. Every question applies the method to that project. There are 70 marks, you have 150 minutes, and you need 42 (60%) to pass. It is open book: the official manual is allowed and you may write notes inside it. There is no negative marking.
teach.cite: PeopleCert PRINCE2 7 Practitioner syllabus, Exam Overview

items.label: standard time (188 min with 25% extra time)

teach.caption: PeopleCert describes it as 56 questions and sub-questions worth 70 marks; the paper numbers every mark from 1 to 70.

teach.h: Where the 70 marks sit, in paper order
teach.caption: Questions are grouped under headings in syllabus order. The practices section is just over half the paper.

rows.label: Options
values: List of 5 or 6 (A to E or F)

rows.label: Option reuse
values: Once, more than once or not at all

teach.caption: Older question styles (assertion-reason, sequence, multiple response) are not used in PRINCE2 7 Practitioner.

teach.body: The booklet gives the background; each question then adds its own short situation. The instructions tell you not to use information from one question to answer another, so a fact from question 20 does not exist in question 21. The additional information about people is needed for at least one question, typically a matching set asking which individual best suits a role. Read it once early, then return to it when a question names people.

steps.label: Situation
steps.sub: Which process or stage? Who did what?

steps.label: What is tested
steps.sub: The principle, practice or activity in quotes

steps.label: Verdict
steps.sub: Appropriate or not, from the facts given

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: The option that explains this situation

teach.caption: Most classic stems end 'and why?': you need the right verdict and the reason that fits.

teach.body: Calderbrook Borough Council (scenario S1) is in initiating a project. Project manager Hannah Okoro proposes fortnightly highlight reports to match Kestrel Lane's two-week sprints, reviewed online by the board, and records this in the PID. Asked whether this is an appropriate use of 'agree the tailoring requirements', you would say yes: report frequency and formality are fitted to the project, and the tailoring is documented and agreed during initiation.

teach.h: A matching set on S1: who fits each role?
head: Role
Best individual
Clue in additional information
rows: Commits the agency, owns technical quality
Independent reviewer, no role in parking
teach.caption: Unused options (for example Tom Achebe, who leads the Scrum team) are allowed: some options fit no row.

teach.text: Do not cross options off a matching list as you use them. Each heading or person can be the answer to more than one row, or to none. And remember the tailoring trap behind many format examples: the method, its products and roles can be tailored; the principles and the role rules (one executive, executive never combined with project manager) cannot.

items: 70 marks, 150 minutes (188 with extra time), 42 to pass, no negative marking, open book.
Sections run principles (7), people (6), practices (36), processes (21).
Classic: 1 mark, four options. Matching: 3 rows of 1 mark, options reusable.
Each question stands alone with the booklet; use the additional information for people questions.
Decide the verdict from the facts, then choose the reason that explains it.

summary: You can now describe how the Practitioner paper is built, from the scenario booklet and additional information to classic and matching items. You can also use that structure to answer tailoring and initiation questions on the S1 scenario.

A.q: A candidate reaches the business case section of the Practitioner paper. It shows three statements, a list of five headings (A to E) and an instruction to choose one heading for each statement. How is this item marked, and how should the headings be treated?
options: Three marks; a heading may be chosen for more than one statement
One mark; each heading may be chosen for one statement at most
Three marks; each heading may be chosen for one statement at most
One mark; all three statements must be right to gain the mark
A.why: A matching set is worth 3 marks, one for each row, and each option can be used once, more than once or not at all.

whyNot.1: A matching set carries three marks, one per row, and headings can be reused.
whyNot.2: The mark count is right but options are not limited to one use in a matching set.
whyNot.3: Each row is marked separately; there is no all-or-nothing mark.

A.q: Calderbrook Borough Council is in the 'initiating a project' process for Permits Online. The project manager proposes fortnightly highlight reports to match the supplier's two-week sprints, reviewed by the board online, and records this in the PID. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: 'Tailor to suit the project', because reporting should fit how the project works
'Tailor to suit the project', because each principle can be adapted to fit the project
'Manage by exception', because the board should receive regular reports on progress
'Manage by stages', because the board should review the project at set intervals
A.why: Adjusting the frequency and formality of reports to the project's context is tailoring (2.7), and it is documented and agreed in initiation.

whyNot.1: Right principle, wrong reason: the method is tailored, but the principles themselves are not.
whyNot.2: Manage by exception is about tolerances and escalation, not the format or rhythm of highlight reports.
whyNot.3: Manage by stages provides decision points at stage ends; it does not explain changing the report rhythm.

A.q: During initiation of Calderbrook's Permits Online project, the project manager checks that the project plan, the full business case and the management approaches are consistent with each other before submitting them to the board as one set. Which initiating a project activity is she carrying out?
options: Establish project controls
Agree the management approaches
Assemble the PID
Request project authorization
A.why: Assembling the PID includes cross-checking its elements for compatibility; the version used for authorization is then baselined (15.4.6).

whyNot.0: Establishing project controls agrees the board's level of control and the mechanisms, not the cross-check of the whole set.
whyNot.1: Agreeing the management approaches defines the nine approaches; it comes before the PID is assembled.
whyNot.3: Requesting authorization happens after the PID is assembled and checked.

B.q: Calderbrook's chief executive's office wants Permits Online to use the council's own document templates and to call the senior user the 'service owner'. The project manager wants this agreed and documented before the management approaches are drafted. In which activity should this be done?
options: Agree the management approaches
Agree the tailoring requirements
Establish project controls
Assemble the project initiation documentation
B.why: 'Agree the tailoring requirements' is the first initiation activity: how the method is adapted (terms, templates) is documented and agreed (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: This activity defines the nine management approaches, which follow the tailoring decisions.
whyNot.2: Project controls set the board's level of control and reporting mechanisms, not terminology and templates.
whyNot.3: The PID records the tailoring later; the decision itself is made in 'agree the tailoring requirements'.

B.q: A matching set on the Calderbrook scenario asks who should be the executive. The candidates include Graham Pell (director, budget holder, named accountable in the mandate), Ruth Abernethy (head of the service that will run the product), Siobhan Kerr (supplier's delivery director) and Priya Lal (independent digital assurance lead). Who is the best fit?
options: Ruth Abernethy, who will run the new service
Siobhan Kerr, who is accountable for the build
Graham Pell, the accountable budget holder
Priya Lal, who reviews every digital project
B.why: The executive is the single point of accountability who secures funding and owns the business case; the budget holder named as accountable fits best.

whyNot.0: As the head of the service that will use the product, she fits the senior user role.
whyNot.1: The supplier's delivery director represents supplier interests: a senior supplier.
whyNot.3: An independent reviewer fits project assurance, not the executive.

B.q: In the Practitioner exam, question 31 states that the Calderbrook board has delegated a change budget. Question 33 describes a different request for change and does not mention any change budget. A candidate uses the change budget from question 31 to answer question 33. Is this sound technique, and why?
options: Yes, because every question describes the same project in the booklet
Yes, because later questions in a section build on earlier ones
No, because each question is answered using the booklet and its stem
No, because the additional information replaces facts given in stems
B.why: The instructions say not to use information from one question to answer another: each question stands alone with the scenario booklet.

whyNot.0: The project is shared, but facts added in one question's situation do not carry over to another.
whyNot.1: Questions are independent; they do not build on each other.
whyNot.3: The additional information adds background on people; it does not override a question's own situation.

C.q: During initiation of Permits Online, the project manager proposes that, to speed up decisions, the executive role be shared between the director Graham Pell and councillor Margaret Doyle, so that either can approve a stage plan. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because roles can be combined, split or added when tailoring
Yes, because tailoring decisions are documented and agreed in the PID
No, because tailoring is agreed in starting up rather than in initiation
No, because the executive role is held by one person, even when tailored
C.why: Tailoring cannot break the role rules: there is exactly one executive, a single point of accountability (2.7, 6.2.4).

whyNot.0: True that roles can be tailored, but this does not explain sharing a role that must stay with one person.
whyNot.1: True that tailoring is recorded in the PID, but documenting a change does not make it acceptable.
whyNot.2: Tailoring requirements are agreed in initiating a project, so this reason is wrong.

C.q: In Calderbrook's initiation stage, the project manager prepares the full business case by updating the outline version with time and costs from the newly prepared project plan and the aggregated risks from the project log. She consults project assurance, and Graham Pell, the executive, is accountable. Is this an appropriate application of 'prepare the full business case', and why?
options: Yes, because the full case uses the project plan and the project's risks
Yes, because the business layer is responsible for preparing the full case
No, because the project plan is prepared after the full business case
No, because project assurance is not involved in this activity
C.why: The full business case is built from the outline version using the project plan's time and costs and aggregated risks; the PM is responsible, the executive accountable and assurance consulted (15.4.5).

whyNot.1: The business layer is not involved in this activity; the project manager is responsible.
whyNot.2: The project plan is prepared first, and its time and costs feed the full business case.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is consulted when the full business case is prepared.

C.q: At the end of Calderbrook's initiation stage, the board members agree not to hold a meeting. The project manager emails the assembled PID to the board and asks for authority to deliver the project. Is this an appropriate application of 'request project authorization', and why?
options: Yes, because the executive alone decides whether the project is authorized
Yes, because the request can be made with or without a formal meeting
No, because the PID must be presented to the board in a formal meeting
No, because the request should go to the business layer, not the board
C.why: The PM contacts the board to request authority to deliver the project; this can be done with or without a formal meeting (15.4.7).

whyNot.0: The board as a whole authorizes the project in directing a project, not the executive acting alone.
whyNot.2: A formal meeting is not required for this request.
whyNot.3: The request goes to the project board, which authorizes the project.

reteach.title: Think of the paper as a building with four floors
reteach.question: If the paper were a building, which floor would you be on for each question, and what does each floor ask of you?

blocks.body: The ground floor is principles: seven questions, one per principle. Then people: six questions on teams, change and communication. The biggest floor is practices: every practice has a three-row matching set plus two or three classic questions. The top floor is processes: three questions for each of the seven processes. Every floor looks at the same project in the scenario booklet.

blocks.h: The paper from bottom to top
What each item type asks of you

blocks.text: A fact given in one question's situation does not carry over to the next question. Answer each from the booklet and its own stem.

test.q: Two colleagues sit the PRINCE2 7 Practitioner exam on the same day. Amir scores 41 marks out of 70 and Beth scores 42. Which statement about their results is correct?
options: Both passed, as the pass mark is 38 marks
Beth passed; Amir is one mark short
Both passed, as the pass mark is 41 marks
Neither passed, as the pass mark is 49 marks
test.why: The pass mark is 42 out of 70 (60%), so 42 passes and 41 does not.

whyNot.0: 38 was the old 6th edition pass mark (out of 68); PRINCE2 7 needs 42.
whyNot.2: The pass mark is 42, so 41 falls one short.
whyNot.3: 49 is the number of classic questions, not the pass mark.

test.q: A candidate preparing for the Practitioner paper wants to know where the questions on 'managing a stage boundary' will appear, so she can plan her time. Where will they be?
options: In the processes section at the end of the paper
In the progress practice section, before processes
In the principles section, under 'manage by stages'
Spread across every section of the paper
test.why: Process questions form the last section, three per process, after the seven practice sections.

whyNot.1: The progress practice has its own section, but process activity questions sit in the processes section.
whyNot.2: Principle questions test the principles; process activities are tested in the processes section.
whyNot.3: Questions are grouped under headings in syllabus order, not scattered.

explain.body: Classic questions give one situation and four options, worth one mark. Matching sets give three rows and a list of five or six options, one mark per row, with options reusable. There are seven matching sets, one in each practice section.

test.q: A tutor is building a mock Practitioner paper that follows the official blueprint. He needs to place the matching sets. How many should there be, and where?
options: Seven, one in each of the process sections
Seven, one in each of the practice sections
Three, all within the people section
Seven, one in each of the principle questions
test.why: The paper has seven matching sets, one per practice, worth 21 marks in total.

whyNot.0: Process sections contain classic questions, three per process.
whyNot.2: The people section has six classic questions.
whyNot.3: Principles are tested by seven classic questions, one per principle.

explain.body: The additional information lists people with their jobs, history and relationships. Match people to roles on evidence: accountability and budget for the executive, use of the products for the senior user, command of the supplier's resources for the senior supplier, independence for project assurance.

test.q: A matching set on the Calderbrook scenario asks who should be senior supplier. The options include Siobhan Kerr (Kestrel Lane's delivery director, accountable for its staff and technical quality), Tom Achebe (leads Kestrel Lane's Scrum team), Ruth Abernethy (head of parking services) and Priya Lal (independent assurance lead). Who fits best?
options: Tom Achebe
Ruth Abernethy
Priya Lal
Siobhan Kerr
test.why: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality and technical integrity of what the supplier delivers.

whyNot.0: Leading the Scrum team day to day fits the team manager role.
whyNot.1: The head of the service that will use the product fits the senior user role.
whyNot.2: An independent reviewer fits project assurance.
